title: Pope Leo heads to Milei's Argentina as tensions loom over austerity, Iran
text:
Pope Leo heads to Milei's Argentina as tensions loom over austerity, Iran

By Leila Miller and Joshua McElwee

Nov 8, 2026

Add AL-MONITOR on Google

Pope Leo visits Uruguay — ANDRES CUENCA

By Leila Miller and Joshua McElweeFLORIDA, Uruguay, Nov 8 (Reuters) - Pope Leo heads to Argentina on Sunday for the second leg of a 12-day tour across South America, kicking off the visit with a closely watched speech to Argentine President Javier Milei, a libertarian seen as a close ally of Donald Trump.The address by the first US-born pope may underscore tensions between the Vatican and Milei, whose austerity agenda has been criticized by the Church for hitting the poorest hardest. The Argentine leader has also strongly supported the Iran war, which Leo has denounced to Trump's ire.Leo, on an ambitious three-country tour through November 17, is arriving in Argentina from Uruguay, where he urged South American countries to tackle regional issues together and set an example for the value of patient diplomacy over conflict.At his final public event in Uruguay, a Mass with an estimated 50,000 people near rolling hills and vineyards about 100 km (62 miles) north of Montevideo, the pope urged political leaders there to work to benefit the whole country, not a select few."Let us pray for those who bear the responsibility of governing (Uruguay), that they may seek with integrity the good of all," the pope told crowds in Florida, outside a famous Catholic shrine.The 71-year-old pontiff, who is making one of the most intense foreign trips of a Catholic leader in decades less than a month after undergoing lung cancer surgery, will be the first Catholic leader to visit Argentina since 1987 and will tour four cities from Sunday to Wednesday.POPE'S SPEECH WILL BE CAREFULLY PARSEDMilei swept to power in 2023 after a run of center-left Peronist rule, campaigning with a chainsaw as a symbol of the deep cuts to state spending he pledged to make to shore up the country's finances.Leo, who addresses national governments on each of his foreign visits, usually speaks in careful, diplomatic language but has emerged as a more forceful voice on the world stage recently, decrying the direction of global leadership.He is not expected to directly criticize Milei by name but may refer to national policies or international events in remarks that will be carefully parsed by political observers."Any interventions by Leo, particularly on poverty, the limits of markets or confrontational political rhetoric, could be read as implicit criticism of Milei and amplify existing opposition to the government's approach," said Nicolas Watson, a managing director at advisory firm Teneo.Milei has defended his austerity as the only way to bring inflation under control. Under his economic campaign, annual inflation has fallen from over 200% to 33%.But surveys show his popularity has slipped ahead of elections next year as Argentines contend with subsidy cuts, public-sector layoffs and business closures linked to squeezed household budgets.POPE TO VISIT PRISON, DISABILITY CARE CENTEROver his 18-month papacy, Leo has forcefully warned about the risks of artificial intelligence, urged world leaders to treat immigrants more humanely, and called for action to address climate change, appeals that have put him at odds with Trump and other right-wing leaders.Fortunato Mallimaci, a sociologist at Argentina's Conicet research agency, said Leo's visit to Argentina will create a sense of unity and energy among those who feel excluded by Milei's economic program.The pope's itinerary in Argentina includes visits to a care center for people with disabilities and a prison, underscoring his focus on highlighting groups that are often marginalized.Jorge Silanes, religious director of the Pequeño Cottolengo Don Orione care center that will welcome the pope on Monday, said the visit carried added significance because spending cuts have reduced disability benefits while poverty remains widespread.Milei was known for piling insults on Leo's predecessor, Francis, an Argentine who never came home during his 12-year papacy. Despite calling Francis "an imbecile," Milei eventually sought to repair relations and visited the late pope at the Vatican."Milei doesn't win anything by fighting with (Leo)," said Veronica Gimenez Beliveau, a sociologist at the University of Buenos Aires. "He could gain in showing an orderly country and administration," she said. (Reporting by Leila Miller in Buenos Aires and Joshua McElwee in Florida, Uruguay, with additional reporting by Lucila Sigal;Editing by Rod Nickel, Alistair Bell and Helen Popper)
